item.title: Linux Kernel Network Feature Timeline
item.description:
Linux networking evolves through incremental mainline releases rather than separate subsystem releases. The milestones below identify the first stable kernel containing each feature; later kernels may add protocol coverage, drivers, offloads, or userspace interfaces.

Network Feature Quick Facts #

Feature Kernel Release Date Maintainer Page Quick Fact
Netfilter and iptables 2.4.0 January 4, 2001 netfilter.org Netfilter introduced extensible packet-processing hooks, while iptables exposed filtering, NAT, and packet-mangling rules to userspace.
NAPI 2.6.0 December 17, 2003 NAPI combined interrupt notification with polling, thus reducing interrupt overhead when interfaces receive packets at high rates.
CUBIC TCP congestion control 2.6.13 August 28, 2005 CUBIC selects the congestion window from a cubic function of time since the previous congestion event. Linux 2.6.19 later made it the default TCP congestion-control algorithm.
Network namespaces 2.6.24 January 24, 2008 Initial support isolated network devices, protocol stacks, routing tables, firewall rules, and sockets. Subsequent releases expanded device and protocol coverage.
Generic Receive Offload (GRO) 2.6.29 March 23, 2009 GRO aggregates related packets before upper-layer processing, thus amortizing per-packet costs without requiring NIC-specific receive offload.
Receive Packet Steering and Receive Flow Steering 2.6.35 August 1, 2010 RPS distributes receive processing across CPUs in software, while RFS adds flow locality so packet processing can follow the consuming application.
TCP Fast Open client support 3.6 September 30, 2012 TFO can carry application data in the opening SYN when the client has a valid cookie. Server support followed in Linux 3.7.
nftables 3.13 January 20, 2014 nftables project nftables added a programmable packet-classification engine and a Netlink API intended to replace the separate iptables, ip6tables, arptables, and ebtables interfaces.
Extended BPF 3.18 December 7, 2014 eBPF project The bpf() system call and eBPF virtual machine provided the foundation for verified, JIT-compiled programs used by socket filters, traffic control, tracing, and later XDP.
Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) 4.3 November 2, 2015 The VRF device lets interfaces share a network namespace while using separate routing tables, which supports route isolation without creating another namespace.
eXpress Data Path (XDP) 4.8 October 2, 2016 XDP project XDP runs eBPF programs before the kernel allocates a socket buffer, enabling early packet drop, redirection, and load balancing.
BBR congestion control 4.9 December 11, 2016 Google BBR BBR models bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation time instead of treating packet loss as the primary congestion signal.
Kernel TLS transmit offload 4.13 September 3, 2017 kTLS moved TLS record encryption and framing for transmitted data into the kernel. Receive support followed in Linux 4.17.
AF_XDP sockets 4.18 August 12, 2018 XDP project AF_XDP connects XDP programs to userspace through shared-memory rings, supporting copy and zero-copy operation depending on the driver.
Multipath TCP 5.6 March 29, 2020 MPTCP upstream project Initial upstream MPTCP support allowed one logical transport connection to use multiple TCP subflows across different paths.
WireGuard 5.6 March 29, 2020 WireGuard WireGuard added an in-kernel encrypted layer-3 tunnel with a small protocol and cryptographic surface.
IPv6 BIG TCP 5.19 July 31, 2022 BIG TCP allows larger non-GSO packet sizes inside the host stack, thus reducing per-packet overhead on high-speed links. IPv4 support followed in Linux 6.3.

Release dates follow the mainline tags in the Linux kernel Git history. Feature versions are cross-referenced with the KernelNewbies release summaries and the kernel networking documentation.

item.title: iproute2
item.description:
iproute2 is the standard Linux userspace suite for inspecting and configuring the kernel networking stack. The suite covers links, addresses, routes, neighbours, tunnels, traffic control, sockets, hardware offload, and several specialized networking subsystems. Most commands exchange Netlink messages with the kernel; they do not implement the data plane that forwards packets.

The project publishes one release for each Linux kernel release. Matching versions expose the same generation of kernel interfaces, although a newer iproute2 can operate against an older kernel when it does not request unsupported features.

item.title: Linux Packet Filtering with iptables and nftables
item.description:
Linux packet filtering is implemented by Netfilter, a kernel framework that exposes hooks in the networking stack. iptables and nftables are not independent firewalls: they are userspace interfaces for programming packet classification and actions at those hooks.

iptables is the historical interface. Native nftables, configured with the nft command, replaces the separate iptables, ip6tables, arptables, and ebtables rule-management models with one language and one Netlink API. Compatibility tools can still accept iptables syntax while writing to the nftables kernel backend, so the command name alone does not identify the active implementation.

item.title: LXC and Linux System Containers
item.description:
LXC is a userspace interface for Linux containment features. It combines the liblxc library, command-line tools, and distribution templates to create system containers: isolated Linux userspaces that share the host’s kernel.

An LXC container can boot an init system, run several services, maintain persistent package state, and expose virtual network interfaces. The operating model therefore resembles a lightweight Linux machine more than an OCI application container. LXC remains a container runtime, however, because it does not boot a guest kernel or emulate hardware.

item.title: Linux Networking
item.description:
Linux exposes network state through namespace-aware interfaces. Since Linux 2.6.25, /proc/net is a compatibility symlink to /proc/self/net, so it describes the network namespace of the reading process. Modern tools normally use Netlink instead of parsing procfs.

Routes and Netlink #

The IPv4 Forwarding Information Base (FIB) determines where packets are sent. /proc/net/route is a historical view of it; ip route queries and changes the kernel through Netlink. Netlink is a family of message-oriented sockets that lets userspace configure and inspect kernel subsystems without adding a new syscall. Routing, links, addresses, neighbours, traffic control, and Netfilter all use it.

item.title: Linux eBPF
item.description:
eBPF is a verified execution environment in the Linux kernel. Applications load programs and maps, attach programs to kernel-defined hooks, and exchange data through file descriptors. Networking remains an important use, but tracing, security policy, and performance analysis no longer depend on packet capture.

From Packet Filters to Linux Socket Filters #

The design lineage begins with DEC’s packet filter for systems including ULTRIX and DIGITAL UNIX. A process opened a packet-filter device, selected an interface, installed an enfilter instruction sequence with ioctl(), and read accepted link-layer packets. The filter used a stack machine, and multiple consumers were ordered by priority.

item.title: glibc Source Internals and System-Call Wrappers
item.description:
glibc exposes C functions such as read(2) and write(2), while Linux exposes architecture-specific system-call entry conventions. A wrapper bridges those layers: it accepts the public C ABI, follows the selected architecture’s system-call ABI, translates kernel errors, and may implement POSIX thread-cancellation behavior.

Examples below describe the current upstream source tree. A released glibc can select different files or macro definitions, so source inspection must begin with the release and target triple being built.

item.title: Linux Kernel Build System
item.description:
The Linux kernel uses GNU Make and Kbuild to configure, compile, link, and install the kernel and its modules. A normal build starts with a configuration target and then builds the default target:

sh 
make defconfig
make -j"$(nproc)"

The principal result is vmlinux, an ELF executable. Architectures may additionally produce bootable wrappers such as bzImage, zImage, or vmlinuz. Loadable modules are ELF relocatable objects linked into .ko files.

Source and Output Trees #

An in-tree build has identical srctree and objtree. An out-of-tree build keeps generated files separate:

item.title: Linux Kernel Source Tree
item.description:
The Linux source tree separates architecture-independent subsystems from architecture ports, public userspace interfaces, generated build state, tools, and tests. Directory names are a navigation aid rather than an execution model: Kconfig selects configuration, Kbuild selects objects, and the selected objects determine what reaches a particular kernel image.

Top-Level Subsystem Boundaries #

The principal source directories are:

Path Responsibility
arch/ Architecture ports, boot code, MMU and interrupt entry, and low-level ABI support.
block/, fs/, mm/, net/ The block layer; VFS and filesystem implementations; virtual and physical memory management; and networking stacks.
kernel/, init/, ipc/, security/ Core scheduling, locking, signals, tracing, and other kernel facilities; early initialization; IPC; and Linux Security Module infrastructure.
drivers/, sound/, virt/ Device drivers, the sound subsystem, and virtualization support such as KVM. A driver need not expose a struct file_operations; subsystem-specific buses and callbacks are also common.
crypto/, lib/, io_uring/, rust/ Shared cryptographic and library support, asynchronous I/O, and Rust kernel support.
include/, Documentation/, scripts/ Headers, maintained documentation, and Kbuild/Kconfig plus generation and maintenance utilities.
tools/, samples/, usr/ Userspace tools such as perf, example programs, and built-in initramfs generation.

Other top-level material such as certs/ and LICENSES/ supports signing, licensing, or build policy. A source checkout changes over time, so inspect its top-level README, MAINTAINERS, and Documentation/ instead of assuming every release contains the same directories.

item.title: Wayland Display Server
item.description:
Wayland is a display protocol designed for a local client and compositor on the same kernel. A toolkit’s Wayland backend uses libwayland-client to connect to a Unix socket, usually $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/$WAYLAND_DISPLAY such as /run/user/1000/wayland-0.

Protocol Model #

Clients and the compositor exchange typed requests and events for numbered objects such as surfaces, buffers, and input seats. XML protocol definitions generate the marshalling stubs. Clients render into shared-memory or DMA-BUF-backed buffers and submit those buffers to the compositor, which combines surfaces and controls outputs and input. A Wayland compositor therefore combines roles that were often separate in an X11 server, window manager, and compositor.

item.title: Linux x86 Calling Conventions
item.description:
A calling convention is a binary contract for argument placement, results, preserved state, and stack layout. Linux x86-64 programs use the System V AMD64 function ABI; 32-bit programs use the System V i386 ABI. Linux system calls use separate entry ABIs and must not be treated as ordinary function calls.

AMD64 Function Calls #

The AMD64 ABI first classifies each argument. Integer-class values, including ordinary integers and pointers, use rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, and r9. SSE-class values use xmm0 through xmm7. Exhausting one class does not by itself exhaust the other; arguments that cannot be assigned according to the classification rules go in the stack input area.

item.title: Pluggable Authentication Modules
item.description:
Linux-PAM lets an application delegate authentication policy to administrator-controlled modules. The application owns the user interaction and its privilege boundary; PAM owns a transaction handle, loads the configured stack, and combines module results. Consequently, an application can use local passwords, smart cards, directory services, MFA, or account restrictions without embedding those mechanisms.

Transaction Roles #

A PAM transaction has five roles:

  • the application starts and ends the transaction;
  • the service is the policy name supplied to pam_start, commonly login, sshd, or sudo;
  • a management group selects the operation: auth, account, session, or password;
  • a module is a shared object implementing one or more management-group entry points;
  • the conversation function lets a module request prompts, informational messages, and responses through the application.

The application begins with pam_start(service, user, &conversation, &pamh). pam_handle_t is opaque and belongs to one transaction; create another handle for another concurrent transaction. A typical authorization path calls pam_authenticate, optionally pam_setcred, then pam_acct_mgmt; it calls pam_open_session before granting a session and pam_close_session while tearing it down. Password changes use pam_chauthtok. Regardless of the path, the application calls pam_end(pamh, last_status), which invalidates the handle and runs registered cleanup callbacks.

item.title: Password Hashing on Linux
item.description:
Password storage uses a one-way password-hashing function, not encryption. A verifier hashes a submitted password with the settings embedded in the stored value and compares the encoded results. Recovery of a plaintext password is not part of the design; an attacker who obtains the database instead tests candidate passwords offline. Thus, modern password hashing needs a per-password random salt and a deliberately expensive, supported algorithm.

item.title: Linux Kernel Infrastructure
item.description:
Subsystem code depends on infrastructure spread across generic headers, architecture overrides, generated files, and core implementation directories. The following notes organize several mechanisms that do not belong to one device or protocol subsystem: diagnostics, error-valued pointers, branch hints and patchable branches, one-copy accesses, and SLUB allocation paths.

Diagnostics and Error Reporting #

Kernel diagnostics use severity-specific pr_*() macros and device-aware dev_*() macros:

c 
if (revision < minimum_revision) {
 dev_err(dev, "unsupported revision %#x\n", revision);
 return -ENODEV;
}

pr_debug("queue depth: %u\n", depth);

dev_err() includes device context; pr_err() is appropriate when no device exists. Dynamic debug can enable selected pr_debug() and dev_dbg() call sites without promoting permanent log noise. Rate-limited variants such as pr_warn_ratelimited() protect the log from recurring conditions.

item.title: Installing Slackware in QEMU
item.description:
Slackware retains a direct relationship between its mirror tree, installation media, package series, and text-mode installer. Understanding that structure helps when selecting packages and diagnosing an installation. The examples below install Slackware64 15.0 in a UEFI QEMU virtual machine.

Slackware Resources and Mirror Tree #

The primary project resources are:

  • Slackware Linux for release announcements and project information
  • Slackware Documentation Project for installation and administration documentation
  • Slackware Linux Essentials for the SlackBook
  • Slackware mirrors and the mirror list for release files

A mirror root contains historical releases, stable-release aliases, development trees, ISO images, and unsupported additions:

item.title: Linux TUN/TAP
item.description:
TUN/TAP creates virtual network interfaces connected to a userspace file descriptor. A TUN device carries layer-3 IP packets; a TAP device carries layer-2 Ethernet frames. They are used by VPNs, packet analyzers, userspace network stacks, and virtual machines.

Creating an Interface #

Open /dev/net/tun read-write and issue TUNSETIFF with an ifreq. Set IFF_TUN or IFF_TAP; add IFF_NO_PI when the program should receive only packets or frames. Without IFF_NO_PI, each read starts with a four-byte packet-information header containing flags and protocol. The kernel creates the network interface, after which ip link, ip address, and ip route configure its administrative state, addresses, and routes.

item.title: Bash
item.description:
Bash is both an interactive command language and a scripting runtime. Reliable shell code treats words, exit statuses, and file descriptors as distinct data flows. Start scripts with an explicit interpreter when Bash features are required:

bash 
#!/usr/bin/env bash

bash -c 'commands' name arg1 assigns name to $0 and arg1 to $1. That detail matters when a command string consumes positional parameters.

Shell Grammar and Execution #

A list joins pipelines with ;, &, &&, or ||. && and || are short-circuit operators; & starts an asynchronous list. A pipeline joins commands with |, or with |& when the left command’s standard error is also sent to the pipe.

item.title: Linux Kernel Locking
item.description:
Kernel locking begins with execution context. A lock that is correct between process-context callers can deadlock when the same data is reached from a softirq, hard interrupt, or nonmaskable interrupt (NMI). The primitive and its suffix must match every context that accesses the protected state.

Spin-Lock Semantics #

Declare and initialize ordinary spin locks with:

c 
static DEFINE_SPINLOCK(queue_lock);

struct queue {
 spinlock_t lock;
};

spin_lock_init(&queue->lock);

On a non-PREEMPT_RT SMP kernel, spin_lock() disables preemption on the local CPU and spins until it acquires exclusive ownership. It does not disable local interrupts or softirqs. A holder must not sleep, schedule explicitly, perform a blocking allocation, or call code that can acquire a sleeping lock.

item.title: Linux Randomness APIs
item.description:
Randomness APIs serve two different contracts. Deterministic pseudo-random number generators are useful for repeatable tests and simulations. Security-sensitive keys, nonces, tokens, salts, and seeds require bytes from the kernel’s cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG).

C Library Generators #

rand() advances hidden process state and returns an integer from 0 through RAND_MAX. srand(seed) selects a repeatable sequence for a particular C library implementation; omitting it behaves as though the seed were 1. ISO C does not specify the algorithm or require the same sequence across implementations, so a test that needs cross-platform reproducibility should choose and record an explicit algorithm.

item.title: Linux Kernel Virtualization
item.description:
KVM exposes Linux hardware virtualization through /dev/kvm. KVM supplies the kernel execution mechanism, while a virtual machine monitor such as QEMU constructs and operates a complete guest machine.

Division of Responsibilities #

KVM uses Intel VT-x, AMD-V, Arm virtualization extensions, or the corresponding host facility to execute guest instructions directly when possible. Kernel code manages vCPU state, second-stage memory translation, interrupt delivery, timers, and transitions between guest and host execution. KVM intentionally does not provide a complete firmware and device model.

item.title: ELF Format
item.description:
ELF is the object and executable format used by Linux and many Unix-like systems. Its ELF header locates the program-header table, used by the loader, and the section-header table, used mainly by linkers and other tooling.

Sections #

Sections organize object-file content such as code, data, symbols, relocations, and string tables. They are not the same as loadable segments: a linker groups sections into segments according to the runtime memory layout.

item.title: Linux System Calls
item.description:
Linux system calls form an architecture-specific binary interface between a process and the kernel. Application code normally targets a C library API instead, because the library supplies types, feature-test macros, compatibility behavior, and the machine-specific entry sequence.

Library API and Kernel ABI #

A source-level call such as open(path, flags) is not a promise to execute a kernel system call named open. glibc can implement it with openat, add cancellation checks, or select a time-width-compatible entry point. Functions such as clock_gettime can execute in the vDSO without entering the kernel. Conversely, Linux exposes system calls such as gettid for which older C libraries did not provide a wrapper.

item.title: awk
item.description:
awk transforms text as a stream of records. Each record is tested against ordered pattern-action rules, which makes the language suited to reports, validation, and small data transformations. POSIX awk is widely available; GNU awk (gawk) adds features that scripts should declare when they require them.

Records, Fields, and Counters #

RS separates input records and defaults to newline. FS separates fields; its default treats runs of spaces and tabs specially. $0 is the whole record, $1 through $NF are fields, and NF is the field count. NR counts records across all inputs, whereas FNR restarts for each input file.

item.title: systemd
item.description:
systemd is a service manager and a suite of Linux system-management components. The system manager runs as PID 1; per-user managers run as systemd --user. Both managers load units, calculate transactions of jobs, and supervise process groups through Linux control groups.

Units, Jobs, and Lifecycle States #

A unit represents a resource known to a manager. Common unit types are:

Suffix Resource
.service A process or daemon
.socket An IPC or network socket used for activation
.target A synchronization and grouping point
.mount, .automount, .swap Storage configuration
.device, .path, .timer Device or event-based activation
.slice, .scope cgroup organization and externally started processes

A job is a requested unit state change such as start, stop, or reload. Starting one unit can pull in other jobs; the manager combines them into a transaction, checks for ordering cycles and conflicting jobs, and then dispatches independent work in parallel.

item.title: Man Pages
item.description:
Manual pages are reference documents installed with software. Section numbers distinguish subjects: section 1 documents user commands, 2 system calls, 3 library functions, 4 device and special files, 5 file formats and conventions, 7 overviews and protocols, and 8 administrative commands. A qualified lookup selects the intended page:

sh 
man 2 open
man 3 printf
man 5 passwd

Sections, Names, and Synopses #

Select a page by both name and section because the same name can describe a command, function, or file. Page source and installed filenames conventionally use name.section, such as printf.1 and printf.3. The NAME section provides name \- one-line description; tools such as apropos index that line. The SYNOPSIS follows command-line notation for commands and declaration notation for APIs.

item.title: Linux Printing
item.description:
CUPS provides an Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) client and scheduler. A CUPS destination is a named printer queue or class; a physical or network printer is the device reached by that queue. Consequently, queue state, job state, and device reachability are separate diagnostic concerns.

Queues, Printers, and IPP #

Clients encode job documents and attributes in IPP requests. A local client commonly connects to the scheduler over a Unix-domain socket, while a remote client uses ipp:// or encrypted ipps://, conventionally on TCP port 631. The scheduler spools the job, selects a destination, converts data when required, and sends output through a backend or a driverless IPP connection.

item.title: C Library and glibc History
item.description: Linux applications depend on two different interfaces: the kernel system-call ABI and a C library. The ABI defines the transition into the kernel for a particular architecture. A C library implements the ISO C and POSIX interfaces that programs compile against, and it adds the process-startup code, dynamic loader, name-service lookup, threading support, locale handling, and many interfaces that do not map to one system call. The kernel therefore does not provide a complete C runtime.

item.title: QEMU
item.description:
QEMU provides system emulators, user-mode CPU emulators, and storage tools. A system emulator models a complete machine, including CPUs, memory, firmware, buses, and devices. A user-mode emulator translates a foreign-architecture userspace program and maps its system calls to the host kernel; it does not boot a guest kernel.

System Emulation #

qemu-system-x86_64 creates an x86-64 virtual machine. -m selects guest memory and -smp selects virtual CPUs. Firmware is part of the machine configuration: SeaBIOS provides legacy BIOS on x86, while OVMF provides UEFI firmware. Storage backends and devices are distinct: -blockdev defines a backend and -device attaches a guest controller or device. -drive is a convenient shorthand for common combinations.

item.title: Linux Process Model
item.description:
The kernel represents every schedulable flow of execution with struct task_struct, declared in the kernel source’s include/linux/sched.h. Distribution headers in /usr/include/linux are exported userspace ABI headers, not a copy of every kernel internal definition.

Tasks, Threads, and IDs #

A pid_t is an integer type; its width is architecture and ABI dependent. A struct pid represents an identity across PID namespaces and associates numeric PIDs with their namespaces. A task’s pid identifies that individual task in its active namespace. Its tgid is the thread-group ID: for the leader it equals pid, and getpid(2) returns the thread-group ID.

item.title: Linux Administration Notes
item.description:
This collection covers several independent administration tasks: removable storage, capabilities, filesystem locations, image composition, and ELF symbol versions. Each section states the operational boundary that matters for automation.

Operating Removable Devices Safely #

Unmount every mounted filesystem before powering down removable media. udisksctl uses the UDisks service, so it applies desktop-session authorization and coordinates the operation instead of issuing an unmediated device command.

bash 
lsblk -o NAME,PATH,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
udisksctl unmount -b /dev/sdb1
udisksctl power-off -b /dev/sdb

Pass a partition such as /dev/sdb1 to unmount, but pass the whole drive such as /dev/sdb to power-off. The latter flushes buffers, removes the device from kernel use, and, when the hardware supports it, switches off the drive. Verify device names immediately before running the command because names can change across attachment events. A successful unmount alone does not guarantee that a USB enclosure has been powered off.

item.title: Xorg Display Server
item.description:
Xorg is an X11 display server. GUI programs use toolkits such as GTK or Qt and client libraries such as libX11 or libxcb to send X11 requests to it. The server manages input, outputs, and rendering; extensions such as GLX and XRender support accelerated rendering.

Connecting to a Display #

DISPLAY has the form [protocol/]host:display[.screen]. For the usual local display, :0 selects /tmp/.X11-unix/X0. TCP displays use port 6000 + display, though modern Xorg usually disables TCP listening. Once connected, the client and server exchange setup data, requests and replies, and asynchronous events such as key presses and expose notifications. SSH X11 forwarding creates a protected transport while retaining the protocol.

item.title: POSIX Time APIs
item.description:
Time APIs answer different questions: civil time names an instant, monotonic time measures an interval, and CPU clocks measure execution consumed by work. Selecting the wrong clock makes timeouts react to wall-clock corrections or makes I/O waits disappear from measurements.

Clock Selection #

clock_gettime reads a clockid_t into struct timespec, whose tv_sec and tv_nsec fields represent seconds and nanoseconds. POSIX requires CLOCK_REALTIME, the system civil clock measured from the Epoch, and CLOCK_MONOTONIC, whose origin is unspecified and cannot be set. Use realtime for timestamps and monotonic time for elapsed durations and deadlines.

item.title: Linux Virtual Memory
item.description:
Linux virtual memory gives each process a protected virtual address space while letting the kernel share files, overcommit address space, reclaim physical pages, and place memory on NUMA nodes. The discussion assumes a memory-management unit (MMU); Linux has a separate nommu implementation for systems without one.

Translation and TLBs #

Every load, store, and instruction fetch uses a virtual address. Hardware page tables translate the address to a physical page frame plus an offset. Linux models the hierarchy with five levels:

item.title: Name Service Switch
item.description:
The GNU C Library’s Name Service Switch (NSS) separates an application’s lookup API from the data source that answers it. Code calls getpwnam(3), getgrnam(3), getaddrinfo(3), or getservbyname(3); glibc selects and combines services according to /etc/nsswitch.conf. Consequently, a local file, DNS server, directory service, or system service can provide the same category of information without changing callers.

Database Families #

glibc recognizes databases including passwd, group, shadow, hosts, networks, protocols, services, rpc, ethers, netgroup, aliases, publickey, and initgroups. Each has its own libc interfaces and record shape.

item.title: POSIX Threads
item.description:
POSIX threads provide concurrency in one process and one address space. Shared address space does not make shared mutable state safe: mutexes, condition variables, or C atomics must establish ownership and memory visibility.

Creation, Termination, and Cancellation #

pthread_create starts void *(*start_routine)(void *) with one pointer argument. It returns an error number directly, not through errno. A thread terminates by returning from its start routine, calling pthread_exit, or acting on cancellation; returning is equivalent to pthread_exit with that return value. Calling exit or returning from main terminates the entire process, whereas pthread_exit in the initial thread leaves other threads running.

item.title: Linux Seccomp
item.description:
Seccomp (secure computing) restricts the system calls a process may make. In strict mode, a process is limited to a small set of calls, historically read, write, _exit, and sigreturn on existing file descriptors. It is intentionally too narrow for most modern applications.

Filter mode attaches a classic BPF program that examines syscall numbers and selected arguments. The filter can allow, deny with an errno, kill the process, log, trace, or delegate a decision to a userspace notifier. Filters are monotonic: once installed, they cannot be relaxed. no_new_privs is normally required before an unprivileged process installs a filter, preventing the filter from being bypassed through a later privilege gain. Container runtimes use seccomp as one layer of defense, alongside namespaces, capabilities, and mandatory-access-control policy.

item.title: Disabling IPv6
item.description:
Disabling IPv6 removes IPv6-only reachability and can break loopback, container, DNS, and application assumptions. Diagnose address selection and connectivity before treating it as the remedy for a timeout.

Diagnose Address Selection First #

Name resolution can return both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses. A dual-stack client uses address-selection and connection-fallback logic; a failure can instead indicate DNS, a route, firewall policy, path MTU discovery, or a service bound only to IPv4.

item.title: util-linux
item.description:
util-linux is a collection of system utilities maintained as an independent upstream project. It supplies interfaces for block devices, mounts, terminals, sessions, namespaces, resource control, and data formatting. Distributions can split utilities into separate packages, so installed commands depend on packaging policy.

Operational Boundaries #

Commands that modify partitions, mounts, swap, device state, process credentials, or namespaces require suitable privileges. Inspect state before changing it, identify devices through stable attributes such as UUID or /dev/disk/by-id, and confirm a target is not mounted or in active use.

item.title: Linux Kernel Data Structures
item.description:
Linux’s list APIs are intrusive: linkage is embedded in the object owned by a subsystem. Intrusion removes a separate node allocation and lets one object participate in several indexes, but the container API does not own memory or provide synchronization.

Circular Doubly Linked Lists #

struct list_head contains only links:

c 
struct list_head {
 struct list_head *next, *prev;
};

struct job {
 unsigned long id;
 struct list_head pending_link;
 struct list_head owner_link;
};

A list head has the same type as an embedded node. In an empty list, next and prev both point back to the head. In a nonempty list, following either direction eventually returns to the head. Because the head is a sentinel rather than a payload object, iteration has no null terminator.

item.title: Linux GUI Applications in Containers
item.description:
Containers do not automatically have access to the host display session. A GUI client needs the appropriate display socket, environment variables, and credentials; exposing them grants the container meaningful control over the user session and should be done only for trusted images.

X11 #

For X11, mount the host socket directory—typically /tmp/.X11-unix—and pass DISPLAY. The client also needs the matching Xauthority cookie, usually supplied by mounting a narrowly scoped cookie file and setting XAUTHORITY. Do not use xhost +; it disables access control for the display. X11Docker can create a more constrained wrapper around this setup.

item.title: Linux Audio Architecture
item.description: Linux audio is a stack rather than one interchangeable API. ALSA exposes kernel sound devices and a user-space library. PulseAudio or PipeWire can then share those devices among applications, convert formats, mix streams, and apply desktop routing policy. Troubleshooting becomes deterministic when each layer is tested in signal-flow order.

item.title: Linux Keyboard Input
item.description:
Linux separates a keyboard’s transport-level report from a stable input key code and from the text or action produced by a keyboard layout. Keeping those layers distinct explains why a PS/2 and a USB keyboard can generate different hardware data but both report KEY_F.

Overview #

Input follows four conceptual stages:

  1. A transport driver receives bytes or reports. The atkbd driver handles AT and PS/2 scan-code sets, while usbhid parses USB HID usages.
  2. The driver parses make, break, prefix, and repeat state, then reports a Linux input key code such as KEY_F (33) with a press, release, or repeat value.
  3. The input core publishes events through evdev. A graphical compositor or input library normally applies its own layout to these events.
  4. For a Linux virtual console, the kernel keyboard layer applies the active console keymap and emits bytes, Unicode characters, strings, or console actions to the terminal layer.

A scan code is therefore not a character, and a Linux key code is not an X11, Wayland, or Unicode code point.

item.title: Linux CPU Frequency Scaling
item.description:
Modern processors expose performance states that trade execution capacity against power and heat. Linux presents those controls through CPUFreq. “Frequency” remains in the interface for compatibility, although hardware-managed Intel HWP and AMD CPPC operate on performance requests rather than a discrete clock table.

CPUFreq’s Three Layers #

CPUFreq consists of:

  1. The core, which owns policy objects and the common sysfs interface.
  2. Governors, which convert workload demand into performance requests.
  3. Scaling drivers, which translate requests into platform-specific register, firmware, or hardware operations.

Only one struct cpufreq_driver can be registered at a time. The driver must therefore handle every CPU for which CPUFreq is available; heterogeneous systems still use policy objects to represent different control domains.

item.title: Linux Control Groups Version 2
item.description:
Control groups (cgroups) account for and control sets of Linux tasks. A cgroup is not a process-tree node: a task inherits its parent’s cgroup when it forks, but a manager can subsequently migrate it. Consequently, cgroups provide the resource boundary behind service managers and containers, while namespaces provide views of global resources.

This article describes cgroup version 2 (cgroup v2). Its documented interface is the cgroup2 filesystem; files and supported controllers depend on the running kernel configuration and available hardware.

item.title: Linux Kconfig
item.description:
Kconfig describes the choices from which a Linux kernel configuration is built. Kernel developers edit Kconfig files to define symbols and their relationships; users select values through front ends such as make menuconfig, make nconfig, make xconfig, or noninteractive targets such as olddefconfig.

The resulting .config is an input to Kbuild, not a complete build script. Configuration synchronization generates files consumed by Make and C, including include/config/auto.conf and include/generated/autoconf.h.

item.title: Building and Starting Xorg
item.description:
The X.Org projects are hosted at https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/. The xorg/xserver project builds the X server executables, including X and Xorg. The xorg/app/xinit project builds xinit and its startx wrapper.

Starting a Session #

startx invokes xinit, which starts an X server and then a client session. With no explicit client script, it uses the conventional user configuration or system defaults. The server normally creates a local Unix socket such as /tmp/.X11-unix/X0 and sets a corresponding display number. Desktop display managers perform the same broad tasks but additionally manage login, seats, and session lifetime.

item.title: Kubernetes from Scratch
item.description:
Building Kubernetes from source is suitable for studying or testing a patched component. A production cluster also requires a supported upgrade path, certificate rotation, backup recovery, networking, storage, monitoring, and incident procedures.

Object Model and API Paths #

Kubernetes models cluster operations as CRUD on resources. Each object has a UID, a type, a unique name within that type, labels for indexed selection, and annotations for non-identifying metadata.

item.title: Linux Socket System
item.description:
A socket is a file descriptor representing one endpoint of a communications channel. Programs create one with socket(2), then usually bind or connect it and use read(2)/write(2) or send(2)/recv(2).

c 
int sockfd = socket(int domain, int type, int protocol);

The domain selects an address family such as AF_INET, AF_INET6, AF_UNIX, or AF_NETLINK. The type selects a semantic such as SOCK_STREAM, SOCK_DGRAM, or SOCK_SEQPACKET; the protocol normally selects a concrete protocol within that combination, or 0 selects the default.

item.title: Android System Architecture
item.description:
Android uses the Linux kernel for scheduling, process isolation, device drivers, networking, and filesystems, but supplies its own native library, runtime, framework, and application model. Bionic is Android’s C library. ART executes DEX bytecode, and Binder provides the principal cross-process RPC mechanism.

Runtime and Process Creation #

Build tools compile Java or Kotlin sources to class files and then transform them into DEX code. An APK or app bundle delivery split packages DEX, resources, native libraries, signing metadata, and a manifest. ART compiles and interprets DEX as appropriate for the device and profile state; an APK is not simply an executable JAR.

item.title: Linux Namespaces
item.description:
Namespaces partition names and resource views that would otherwise be global. Each task has one namespace instance of each supported type, and tasks in the same instance observe the same instance-specific resources. Namespaces do not, by themselves, constrain CPU, memory, or I/O consumption; cgroups provide those resource controls.

Linux exposes eight namespace types. Time namespaces were added in Linux 5.6; the other types predate that release. The namespace flags in include/uapi/linux/sched.h are the version-specific source of truth.

item.title: Linux File Descriptors
item.description:
Linux separates a process’s integer handle from the kernel object that stores an open instance’s state. The distinction explains offset sharing, duplication, inheritance, and many descriptor leaks.

Descriptor Tables and Open-File Descriptions #

A file descriptor is a nonnegative integer indexing the calling process’s descriptor table. A table entry references an open-file description, represented inside Linux by struct file. The open-file description records state such as:

  • the current file offset;
  • file status flags such as O_APPEND and O_NONBLOCK;
  • the opened path, access mode, credentials, and file operations.

item.title: Linux Kernel Release Lifecycle
item.description:
Linux development follows a time-based cycle around the mainline Git tree maintained by Linus Torvalds. Mainline development, stable backports, and distribution kernels are related but distinct release streams.

Mainline Development #

Most patches move through a hierarchy rather than going directly to Linus. A developer posts a patch to the relevant mailing list; reviewers and a subsystem maintainer evaluate it; the maintainer stages accepted work in a subsystem tree. Lower-level trees can feed higher-level trees, such as a driver tree feeding a networking tree. Integration in linux-next exposes conflicts between subsystem trees before they reach mainline. During the merge window, top-level maintainers send signed pull requests to Linus’s tree.

item.title: GNOME Development Environment
item.description: Debugging across GLib and GTK requires a consistent dependency graph. If GTK loads a development libgtk but resolves GLib, Pango, or GDK Pixbuf from the host, source lines and runtime types no longer correspond to one coherent build. An isolated installation prefix provides that consistency without replacing distribution packages.

item.title: Virtual File Systems
item.description:
Linux uses filesystem interfaces for both stored data and live kernel state. The Virtual Filesystem Switch (VFS) makes those objects accessible through common system calls, while pseudo-filesystems such as procfs and sysfs generate their contents from kernel objects. item.title: Supervisord
item.description:
Supervisor is a process-control system for Unix-like hosts. It starts configured programs, captures their output, restarts them when appropriate, and exposes a control interface. It is useful when an application needs a lightweight, explicit process manager, but it is not a substitute for the operating system’s init system or service manager.

Define a Program #

A minimal program definition belongs in Supervisor’s included configuration directory:

ini 
[program:worker]
command=/opt/app/bin/worker --queue=default
directory=/opt/app
user=app
autostart=true
autorestart=unexpected
startsecs=5
stopasgroup=true
killasgroup=true
stdout_logfile=/var/log/app/worker.log
stderr_logfile=/var/log/app/worker-error.log

startsecs prevents a process that exits immediately from being reported as successfully started. stopasgroup and killasgroup help ensure that child processes receive termination signals during a restart. Run the service as an unprivileged user and grant only the filesystem access it needs.

item.title: glibc User Databases
item.description:
The user database maps login names and numeric user IDs to account records. /etc/passwd is the familiar representation, but an application must not assume that the file is the authoritative source. glibc resolves the passwd database through the Name Service Switch (NSS), whose passwd: entry in /etc/nsswitch.conf can consult local files, systemd, LDAP, NIS, or other installed providers.

PAM does not perform these lookups. PAM handles authentication and account-management policy, whereas NSS answers identity database queries.
